To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the BMRE estimator can be used in the presence of observed pleiotropy and that the use of a weakly informative prior can improve power.

1) the BMRE estimator is a powerful approach to correct for pleiotropy in MR analyses, 2) BMRE has a lower susceptibility to InSIDE assumptions compared to MRE, 3) the choice of the prior distribution on the intercept term is crucial to avoid bias in the BMRE slope estimate, 4) the choice of a prior distribution for pleiotropy can be guided by empirical data and a prior distribution for a causal effect of interest.
We propose an alternative implementation of the Mendelian randomization (MR)- Egger (MRE) method, which we call the Bayesian MRE (BMRE) method.
In summary, our research is concerned with
a methodological development of Mendelian randomization (MR) and its application to the study of plasma urate and gout.
the application of the Mendelian randomization method to estimate the effect of a modifiable risk factor on an outcome.
the development and application of a novel Bayesian implementation (BMRE) of the MR-Eger (MRE) IV estimator, to increase power in Mendelian randomisation analyses.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
BMRE is a useful method for dealing with pleiotropy in Mendelian randomization studies, but the user should be cautious in its application.
BMRE is a powerful and useful method for IV analysis, but that the user should be aware of the potential for bias when the InSIDE assumption is violated.
BMRE is a powerful tool for MR, but it should be used with caution and only when the user is certain about the validity of the InSIDE assumptions.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have developed an approach to correct for directional bias in Mendelian randomization (MR) studies, using Bayesian methods to account for pleiotropic effects.
the BMRE is a powerful method that is able to account for observed and unobserved pleiotropy.
the MRE and BMRE methods can be used to detect pleiotropy and to estimate the causal effect, respectively.
The main takeaway from our work is that
a weakly informative prior for the intercept term can be used to improve the precision of the slope estimate.
the use of weakly informative prior distributions may be an attractive alternative to the MRE method to increase power of IV estimates in the presence of observed pleiotropy.
the choice of prior distribution on the intercept term can be used as a tool to balance type 1 error rate, power and robustness to InSIDE assumption violation.
